issues: Whenever a messenger brought him news, he would bestow → 時有報者，輒賜: to the one who then brought the news [of the birth] he at once gave 200 koṭis (Mizutani: その由を知らせる者に直ちに…与えた; Beal similar); name Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi: Mizutani notes the usual form is Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa '20 koṭis', Xuanzang's 二百億 a confusion
en_revised: The country of Īraṇaparvata (伊爛拏鉢伐多國) is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country borders the Ganges River (殑伽河) to the north and is more than twenty li in circuit. The crops are lush and the flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest. There are more than ten monasteries with over four thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Sāmmitīya school. There are more than twenty deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Recently, a neighboring king deposed the ruler of this country and bestowed the capital city upon the community of monks. Within this city, he built two monasteries, each housing nearly one thousand monks, both of which study the Hīnayāna teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school.  Beside the great city, overlooking the Ganges River, is Mount Īraṇa (伊爛拏山), which exhales mists and clouds that obscure the sun and moon. Throughout the ages, immortals and sages have followed one another to dwell here in meditation, and there is now a deva temple that still observes the traditional rites. In the past, the Tathāgata also resided here and preached the profound Dharma extensively for devas and humans. To the south of the great city is a stūpa where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for three months. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the three past Buddhas. Not far to the west of the walking paths of the three Buddhas is a stūpa, which is the birthplace of the bhikṣu Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (室縷多頻設底拘胝). In the past, there was a wealthy and noble elder in this city who had a child late in life. to the one who brought him the news he at once gave two hundred koṭis of gold coins, and thus he named his son "He who heard of the two hundred koṭis" (Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi). By the time he reached adulthood, he had never walked upon the ground, and therefore the hair on the soles of his feet was over a foot long, lustrous, fine, and soft, and the color of yellow gold. Cherishing this son, the elder provided him with every kind of luxury; from his residence all the way to the Snow Mountains, post-stations were linked together and servants lined the roads, so that whenever a rare medicine was required, the word was passed along and the item delivered in succession, arriving in no time at all—such was the extent of his great wealth. The World-Honored One, knowing that his roots of goodness were about to sprout, commanded Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) to go and convert him. Upon arriving at the gate, he had no way to announce himself. The elder’s family worshipped the Sun Deity, and every morning they would face east to bow. At that time, the Venerable One, using his supernatural powers, descended from the solar disc and stood before them. The elder’s son, suspecting he was the Sun Deity, offered him fragrant rice; the Venerable One then returned, and the aroma of the rice filled the entire city of Rājagṛha (王舍城). At that time, King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) was astonished by the extraordinary fragrance and ordered a messenger to investigate; it was discovered that Maudgalyāyana of the Bamboo Grove Monastery (竹林精舍) had brought the rice from the elder’s house, and thus, knowing the elder’s son possessed such a wonder, the king summoned him. The elder accepted the command, but pondered how to travel safely. To travel by boat and row with oars carried the danger of wind and waves; to ride in a carriage or on an elephant brought the fear of stumbling or falling. Thereupon, from his residence to the city of Rājagṛha, he excavated a canal for transport and filled it with mustard seeds, so that the boat could rest securely and be towed along by a long rope. Upon arriving at the city of Rājagṛha, he first paid homage to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said to him, "King Bimbisāra has sent a messenger to summon you for no other reason than to see the hair on the soles of your feet. If the King wishes to view them, you should sit in the cross-legged position. To extend your feet toward the King is, by the laws of the country, a capital offense." The son of the elder received this instruction and went forth, and was led into the court to have an audience. When the king wished to view the hair, he sat in the cross-legged position; the king appreciated his politeness and came to cherish him deeply. Having been permitted to return, he went back to the place of the Buddha. At that time, the Tathāgata (如來) preached the Dharma and provided instruction; upon hearing this, he was moved to realization and immediately renounced the household life. Thereupon, he practiced with diligent effort, seeking to realize the fruits of enlightenment; he engaged in walking meditation without rest until his feet began to bleed. The World-Honored One said to him, "Good man, when you were at home as a layman, did you know how to play the lute?" He replied, "I did." "If that is so, take this as an analogy. If the strings are too tight, the sound will not be in harmony; if the strings are too loose, the melody will not be refined. Neither too tight nor too loose, the sound is then harmonious. The practitioner of the path is also like this. If one is too urgent, the body becomes exhausted and the mind weary; if one is too lax, the passions expand and the will becomes dissipated." Having received the Buddha's instruction, he followed it faithfully, and before long, he attained the realization of the fruit.

issues: Small Isolated Mountain (小孤山; Skt. asura) → the gloss 'Skt. asura' is invented; 小孤山 is simply 'a small isolated hill' (Mizutani: 小さな離れ山; Beal: a small isolated mountain)
en_revised: At the western border of the country, south of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, one reaches the Small Isolated Mountain (小孤山), where the peaks are layered and precipitous. In the past, the Buddha spent three months of the rainy season retreat here, subduing the yakṣa Bakula (薄句羅). On a large rock below the southeastern cliff of the mountain, there is a trace of where the Buddha sat, which is more than an inch deep into the stone, five feet two inches long, and two feet one inch wide; a stūpa has been built upon it. To the south, on another stone, there is a trace of where the Buddha placed his kuṇḍikā (捃稚迦), which is more than an inch deep and shaped like an eight-petaled flower. Not far to the southeast of the Buddha’s sitting trace is the footprint of the yakṣa Bakula, which is one foot five or six inches long, seven or eight inches wide, and slightly less than two inches deep. Behind the yakṣa’s footprint is a stone statue of the seated Buddha, six or seven feet high. Not far to the west is a place where the Buddha walked in meditation. On the summit of the mountain is the former dwelling of the yakṣa. To the north is a footprint of the Buddha, one foot eight inches long, over six inches wide, and about half an inch deep, with a stūpa built over the trace. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued the yakṣa, causing him to cease killing people and eating meat; he respectfully received the Buddha’s precepts and was later reborn in the heavens. To the west of this are six or seven hot springs, the water of which is extremely hot. In the great mountain forests at the southern border of the country, there are many wild elephants, which are immense in size.

issues: shrine (精舍; Skt. mūla-gandha-kuṭī) → gloss invented; 精舍 is just a vihāra/shrine
en_revised: More than twenty li to the west of the city is the Vāśibhā Monastery (跋始婆僧伽藍). Its courtyards and buildings are spacious and open, and its terraces and pavilions are lofty. There are more than seven hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahayana teachings; most of the eminent scholars and renowned monks of East India reside here. Not far to its side is a stupa (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka. This is the place where, in the past, the Tathāgata spent three months preaching the Dharma for the devas and humans; on fast days, it sometimes emits a brilliant light. To its side are the sites of the sitting and walking meditation paths of the four Buddhas. Not far from here is another shrine (精舍), in which is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Its spiritual insight is all-revealing and its divine responses are manifest, so that people from far and near fast and pray before it.

issues: found no errors in the logic or terminology → 一聞究覽，辭義無謬: the śramaṇa, having heard it once, grasped it completely without error in wording or sense (Beal: understood it all … without mistake); mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍) → gloss invented, 精舍 = vihāra; CBETA reads 絡多未知 (未 for 末), DM's 絡多末知 / Raktamṛttikā kept
en_revised: Beside the great city is the Raktamṛttika-saṃghārāma (絡多末知僧伽藍). Its courtyards and buildings are spacious and open, and its towers and pavilions are lofty and steep. The highly talented and profoundly learned scholars of the country, as well as those of renowned intelligence, all assemble therein to assist one another through mutual admonition and to cultivate their morality and virtue.  Formerly, before this country believed in the Buddha-dharma, there was a heretic from South India who bound his belly with copper plates, wore a bright torch upon his head, and, leaning on a staff, walked with proud strides into this city, where he struck the drum of debate and sought to engage in discussion. Someone asked him, "Why do you wear a torch on your head and copper plates on your belly?" He replied, "I have studied so many arts and possess such great ability that I fear my belly might burst; I feel compassion for the ignorant and dark-minded, and that is why I carry a light."  Ten days passed, and no one in the city came forward to question him. The king inquired among the eminent and wise, but there was no one who could match him. The king said, "Within the borders of this realm, can there really be no one of wisdom and clarity? To leave a guest's challenge unanswered is a deep shame for the country. We must search further and inquire among those living in seclusion."  Someone said, "In the great forest there is an extraordinary man who calls himself a śramaṇa; he is dedicated to arduous study and has lived here in quiet seclusion for a long time. Were he not one who embodies the Dharma and accords with virtue, how could he live like this?"  Upon hearing this, the king went in person to invite him. The śramaṇa replied, "I am a man of South India staying here as a traveler; my learning is superficial, and I fear I may fall short of what you have heard. However, I dare to accept your command and will no longer firmly decline. If I am not defeated in the debate, I request that you build a saṃghārāma, gather a community of monks, and glorify and praise the Buddha-dharma." The king said, "I respectfully hear your request and will not dare to forget this virtue." The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and went to the site of the debate. The non-Buddhist then recited his tenets, totaling more than thirty thousand words. Their meaning was profound and their phrasing concise; they encompassed all names and characteristics, capturing the sight and hearing of the audience. The śramaṇa, having heard them once, grasped them completely, without error in wording or meaning, and with a few hundred words, he debated and refuted them, then questioned the non-Buddhist on his tenets. The non-Buddhist, his arguments exhausted and his logic defeated, remained silent and could not respond. Having been defeated in his reputation, he retreated in shame. The king deeply respected the śramaṇa’s virtue and built this saṃghārāma; from that time forward, the Buddha-dharma was widely propagated.  Not far from the side of the saṃghārāma is a stūpa, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for seven days to preach the Dharma and provide guidance. Beside it is a vihāra (精舍), the place where the past four Buddhas sat and walked in meditation, leaving behind traces. There are several stūpas, all of which are places where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, and they were built by King Aśoka.

issues: (折利呾羅城; meaning "Departure") → no such gloss in the CBETA text; dropped
en_revised: On the southeastern border of the country, facing the shore of the great sea, is the city of Caritra (折利呾羅城). It is over twenty *li* in circuit and serves as a thoroughfare and stopping place for seagoing merchants and travelers from distant lands. The city is solid and steep, and contains many rare treasures. Outside the city, five monasteries stand in a row; their terraces and pavilions are lofty, and the sacred images are exquisitely crafted. To the south, the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) is over twenty thousand *li* away; gazing into the distance on a quiet night, one can see the light of the precious pearl atop the Buddha-tooth stūpa of that land, shining clearly like a torch suspended in the air.

issues: great mountain ridge (Pravaragiri) → the name is DM's addition; the text has only 大山嶺
en_revised: On the northern frontier of the country, atop the great mountain ridge, there is a stone stupa over a hundred feet high. It is the place where, at the beginning of the kalpa when the human lifespan was immeasurable, a Pratyekabuddha entered into extinction.

issues: The king, known as Yin-zheng (引正 - Sadvaha) → 引正王 is the Chinese rendering of the same king Sātavāhana (娑多婆訶) named above, not a different name
en_revised: From here, traveling northwest through mountains and forests for more than 1,800 li, one reaches the country of Kosala (憍薩羅國). The country of Kosala is more than 6,000 li in circumference; its borders are surrounded by mountain ranges, and forests and marshes are interconnected. The capital city of the country is over 40 li in circumference. The soil is rich and fertile, and the land is highly productive. Villages and towns are within sight of one another, and the households are prosperous and substantial. The people are large in stature and dark in complexion. Their customs are fierce and impetuous, and their nature is brave and violent. They believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings, and they are highly skilled in the arts. The king is a Kṣatriya. He deeply reveres the Buddhadharma and is profound in his benevolence and compassion. There are more than one hundred saṃghārāmas, with fewer than ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. There are more than seventy Deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Not far to the south of the city is an old saṃghārāma, and beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata once manifested great supernatural powers at this place to subdue heterodox practitioners. Later, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛) resided in this saṃghārāma. At that time, the king of this country was named Sātavāhana (娑多婆訶). He cherished and respected Nāgārjuna, and he guarded the gates of his dwelling. At that time, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆) came from the country of Siṃhala (執師子國) to seek a debate, and he said to the gatekeeper, "Please announce my visit." The gatekeeper then went to report this. Nāgārjuna, already well aware of his reputation, filled a bowl to the brim with water and instructed a disciple, saying, "Take this water and show it to that Deva." When Deva saw the water, he silently dropped a needle into it. The disciple took the bowl and returned, feeling puzzled. Nāgārjuna said, "What did he say?" The disciple replied, "He said nothing, but merely dropped a needle into the water." Nāgārjuna said, "How wise he is, this man! His knowledge of the subtle is divine, and his perception of the minute is second only to a sage. With such magnificent virtue, he should be invited in immediately." The disciple asked, "What do you mean? Is this what you call silent, marvelous eloquence?" Nāgārjuna said, "Water takes the shape of its container, whether square or round; it adapts to the purity or turbidity of its surroundings; it permeates everywhere without gaps, and its clarity is unfathomable. By showing him the full bowl, I compared it to the all-encompassing nature of my own learning; he, in turn, dropped a needle into it, thereby exhausting its depths. This is no ordinary person; he should be summoned at once."  Nāgārjuna’s demeanor was so awe-inspiring that it commanded respect from all, and those who spoke with him would bow their heads in submission. Deva had long admired his reputation and had long hoped to request his instruction. Before he began his studies, he wished to display his own mental acuity, yet he was also deeply intimidated by the master's majesty. He ascended the hall and sat in a secluded spot, discussing the profound mysteries throughout the day with language and logic of the highest clarity. Nāgārjuna said, "Your scholarship surpasses the world and your brilliant eloquence outshines your predecessors. I am but a feeble old man, and meeting such a talented youth truly allows me to pour the contents of my vessel into another and keep the lamp of transmission burning without end; the propagation of the Dharma depends on such a person. I hope you will move to the front seat so that we may discuss the profound mysteries."  Deva, having heard this command, felt a sense of self-assurance. He prepared to open the storehouse of his doctrines and first wandered through the garden of debate, raising the points of his argument and looking up to challenge the master's principles. But suddenly beholding the master's majestic countenance, he was struck speechless and fell silent; he moved from his seat to acknowledge his faults and then requested to become a disciple. Nāgārjuna (龍猛) said: "Sit down again; I shall now bestow upon you the most perfect and wonderful truth, the authentic teachings of the Dharma King." Deva (提婆) prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, single-mindedly took refuge, and said: "From this moment forward, I dare to follow your instructions." Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva was well-versed in the arts of medicine; by consuming elixirs to nourish his life, he lived for several hundred years, his spirit and appearance showing no signs of decline. King Sātavāhana (引正王), having obtained the wonderful medicine, also lived for several hundred years. The king had a young son who said to his mother: "At this rate, when will I ever be able to succeed to the throne?" His mother replied: "Judging by the present situation, there is no prospect of it. Your father the king has already lived for several hundred years, and many of his descendants have already grown old and died. This is all due to the power of Nāgārjuna’s merit and the efficacy of his medical arts. If the Bodhisattva were to pass away, the king would surely perish. Now, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva possesses vast wisdom and profound compassion; he provides for all living beings and regards his own life as something to be cast aside. You should go to him and try to beg for his head; if you can fulfill this intention, your wish will be granted." The prince respectfully obeyed his mother's command and came to the monastery (saṃghārāma); the gatekeepers were awestruck and fearful, so he was able to enter. At that time, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva was reciting scriptures while walking in meditation. Suddenly seeing the prince, he stood still and said to him: "For what reason have you come to this monastery this evening, appearing as if in danger and fear, and rushing here so quickly?" He replied: "I have received the words of my compassionate mother, who spoke of those who practice renunciation. I have thought that for all living beings, their precious life is the most important thing, and in the authoritative words of the scriptures, there has never been anyone who lightly cast aside their physical body to bestow it upon those who seek it." My compassionate mother said: "It is not so. The Sugatas of the ten directions and the Tathāgatas of the three ages, from the time they first resolved their minds until they attained the fruit of enlightenment, diligently sought the Buddha-way and practiced precepts and forbearance. Some threw their bodies to feed hungry beasts, some cut their flesh to save a dove; King Candraprabha gave his head to a Brahmin, and King Maitrībala gave his blood to satisfy hungry Yakṣas; examples such as these are truly difficult to enumerate fully. Among the sages of the past, what age was without such people?" Now, Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩), you are firm in your noble ambitions; I have a request for a human head to use, but though I have sought one for many years, no one has yet offered theirs. To commit a violent robbery and murder would result in many accumulated sins, and to cruelly harm the innocent would make one's defiled virtue manifest. But you, Bodhisattva, practice the holy path and look toward the distant fruit of Buddhahood; your compassion moistens all sentient beings, and your kindness reaches the boundless. You treat life as lightly as a floating thing and consider your body as cheap as rotten wood; do not violate your original vow, but grant what I seek!"  Nāgārjuna said: "Yes, these words are true! I seek the holy fruit of Buddhahood and I learn from the Buddha the ability to renounce; this body is like an echo, this body is like a bubble, circulating through the four types of birth and coming and going through the six realms, bound by a long-standing great vow never to oppose the desires of living beings. However, Prince! There is one thing that is not possible; what shall be done about it? Once my body is finished, your father will also perish; considering this, who will be able to provide for him?" Nāgārjuna paced about and looked around, seeking a way to end his life; he cut his own throat with a blade of dry cogon grass as if with a sharp sword, and his head was severed from his body. The prince, having seen this, fled in terror. The gatekeeper went up and reported, detailing the beginning and the end; the king, upon hearing this, was moved by grief and indeed also passed away.

issues: shrines (*mūla-gandha-kuṭī* 精舍) → gloss invented, 精舍 = vihāras/shrines; The outer openings of the isolated cells illuminate → 疎寮外穴，明燭中宇: windows open to the outside and light the interior (Beal: windows… let in light)
en_revised: Three hundred or more *li* southwest of the country, one arrives at the mountain of Bhramaragiri (跋邏末羅耆釐山). It rises abruptly and loftily, with precipitous peaks and cliffs; having neither slopes nor valleys, it appears to be a single solid rock. King Śātavāha (引正王) excavated this mountain for the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) to establish a monastery. Ten or more *li* away from the mountain, a tunnel was excavated; directly beneath the mountain, they chiseled upward to clear the stone. Within it are long corridors and eaves, lofty terraces and multi-storied pavilions; the pavilions have five tiers, and each tier has four courtyards, all containing shrines (精舍) where golden images of the Buddha's size have been cast with exquisite craftsmanship, while the remaining decorations consist entirely of gold and jewels. From the high peaks of the mountain, a waterfall pours down, flowing around the multi-storied pavilions and winding through the corridors and halls. Windows pierced through to the outside light up the interior.  Initially, when King Śātavāha was building this monastery, the labor force was exhausted and the treasury was empty; with the work not yet half finished, his heart was filled with deep sorrow. Nāgārjuna said to him, "Great King, why are you so burdened with worry?" The king replied, "I have given rise to a great aspiration and ventured to establish a supreme field of merit, hoping it would remain firm forever until the coming of Maitreya (慈氏). With the work not yet finished and the financial resources exhausted, I am constantly filled with this regret, sitting and waiting for the dawn." Nāgārjuna said, "Do not worry. The merit of cultivating such supreme goodness is inexhaustible; if one has raised a vast vow, there is no worry that it will not be fulfilled. Return to the palace today and enjoy yourself to the fullest; tomorrow morning, go out for an excursion to observe the mountains and fields, and then come here to discuss the construction." Having received this instruction, the king followed it and acted accordingly. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛) used a miraculous elixir, dripping it onto various large rocks, which all turned into gold. When the king went on an excursion and saw the gold, he rejoiced in his heart and words; he returned with his carriage to the place of Nāgārjuna and said, "During my hunting excursion today, I was deluded by spirits and ghosts, for in the mountains and forests I repeatedly saw heaps of gold." Nāgārjuna said, "It was not a delusion by ghosts. It was the response to your utmost sincerity; that is why this gold appeared. You should take and use it in time to complete your supreme undertaking." He then used it for the construction, and after the work was finished, there was still a surplus. Thereupon, in each of the five tiers, he cast four large golden statues, and the remainder was still so abundant that it filled the treasuries. He summoned and gathered one thousand monks to reside within and perform rites and chanting. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna collected and classified the teachings proclaimed by the Buddha Śākyamuni and the treatises expounded by the various Bodhisattvas, storing them within. Thus, the first tier at the top housed only Buddha images and various scriptures and treatises; the fifth tier at the bottom was for the residence of lay servants (淨人), property, and miscellaneous goods; and the three middle tiers were the lodgings for the monks. I have heard from the records of former sages that after King Śātavāha (引正王) had completed the construction, the cost of the salt consumed by the workers was calculated to be nine koṭis of gold coins. Later, the monks fell into disputes and went to the king to seek a settlement. At that time, the lay servants said to one another, "Since a quarrel has arisen among the monks and their arguments are contradictory, evil men will watch for an opening to destroy the monastery." Consequently, they barred the multi-storied pavilion and expelled the monks. Since that time, there has been no monastic community. Looking at the mountain cliffs from afar, one cannot discern any gate or path. At that time, they would bring in those skilled in medical arts to treat illnesses, but they were blindfolded upon entering and exiting, so they did not know the route.

issues: From this great forest, traveling south → 從此大林中南行: from here, traveling south through a great forest; built by the arhat Acala (阿折羅) → 並阿折羅阿羅漢之所建: both the monastery and the stūpa were built by the arhat Ācāra (阿折羅; Chinese 所行 'conduct', Mizutani Ācāra); the sanghārāma of the aforementioned arhat → 所行羅漢伽藍: the monastery of the arhat Ācāra (所行 is his Chinese name, not 'aforementioned')
en_revised: From here, traveling south through a great forest for more than nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Āndhra (案達羅國). The country of Āndhra is more than three thousand li in circumference. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circumference and is named Vengīpura (瓶耆羅). The land is fertile and rich, and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and violent. Their language and tone of speech differ from those of Mid-India, but as for their written characters, the rules are largely the same. There are more than twenty sanghārāmas (伽藍) with more than three thousand monks. There are more than thirty deva temples, and the followers of heterodox paths are very numerous. Not far from the side of Vengīpura city is a large sanghārāma with multi-storied pavilions and layered terraces, the craftsmanship of which exhausts the possibilities of carving; the sacred images of the Buddha are of exquisite and ingenious design. In front of the sanghārāma is a stone stūpa several hundred feet high; both were built by the arhat Ācāra (阿折羅). Not far to the southwest of the sanghārāma of the arhat Ācāra (所行) is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王); in the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, manifested great supernatural powers, and saved immeasurable multitudes.

issues: the solitary hill (Vyāsa) → 'Vyāsa' is an invented gloss; 孤山 = a solitary hill
en_revised: Traveling more than twenty li southwest from the monastery of the Arhat Ācāra, one reaches a solitary hill (孤山). On the mountain ridge is a stone stūpa where the Bodhisattva Dignāga composed the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic). This Bodhisattva Dignāga, after the Buddha had passed away, followed the tradition and donned the dyed robes. His wisdom and vows were vast and great, his power of discernment deep and firm; pitying the world for having no refuge, he contemplated propagating the sacred teachings. Thinking that the theories of *hetuvidyā* were profound in language and extensive in reasoning, such that students labored in vain and found it difficult to achieve success, he hid his traces among secluded cliffs and settled his spirit in silent meditation, examining the merits and demerits of past works and scrutinizing the verbosity and conciseness of their meanings. At that time, the cliffs and valleys shook and echoed, the mist and clouds changed color, and a mountain god lifted the Bodhisattva up several hundred feet, proclaiming: "In the past, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, guided sentient beings through skillful means and, with a compassionate heart, preached the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*, encompassing wonderful principles and investigating subtle words to their depths. Since the Tathāgata entered extinction, the great meaning has been cut off. Now, the Bodhisattva Dignāga, whose merit and wisdom are vast and far-reaching, and who deeply understands the sacred intent, shall once again propagate the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* on this day." The Bodhisattva then emitted a great light, illuminating the darkness. At that time, the king of this country felt deep respect; seeing this radiant appearance, he suspected the Bodhisattva had entered the diamond samādhi and therefore requested him to realize the fruit of birthlessness. Dignāga said: "I have entered samādhi to observe and wish to explain the profound scriptures; my heart is set on perfect enlightenment, not on the fruit of birthlessness." The king said: "The fruit of birthlessness is something all sages admire; it severs the desires of the three realms and provides mastery of the three types of supernormal knowledge—this is a magnificent achievement, and I hope you will realize it quickly." At that time, Dignāga was pleased by the king’s request and was about to realize and accept the holy fruit of the non-learner (aśaikṣa). At that moment, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (妙吉祥菩薩) knew of this and felt it was a pity; wishing to warn him, he snapped his fingers to awaken him and said: "What a pity! How can you abandon your vast and great mind for a narrow and inferior aspiration, following a desire for solitary perfection while discarding your vow to benefit others? If you wish to perform a virtuous benefit, you should widely propagate the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (瑜伽師地論) composed by the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩) to guide and encourage later students; the benefit of this is truly great." The Bodhisattva Dignāga respectfully accepted this instruction and followed it accordingly. Thereupon, he pondered deeply and researched extensively the treatises on logic (hetuvidyā). Fearing that students might be intimidated by the subtlety of the text and the conciseness of the language, he extracted the essential meanings and synthesized the subtle words to compose the *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* (因門論) in order to guide those who would come after. From this time forward, he propagated the *Yogācāra*, and his flourishing work and disciples were known throughout the world.

en_revised: Not far to the south of the city is a great mountain crag, the place where the master of treatises Bhāviveka (婆毘吠伽) dwelt in the Asura Palace (阿素洛宮), awaiting the time when the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩) attains Buddhahood. The master of treatises possessed a refined character that was vast and far-reaching, and his ultimate virtue was profound and deep; outwardly he displayed the attire of the Sāṃkhya (僧佉), while inwardly he promoted the teachings of Nāgārjuna (龍猛). Hearing that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法菩薩) in the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國) was propagating the Dharma teachings to thousands of students, he felt a desire to engage in discussion, so he took up his staff and set out. Upon arriving at the city of Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐城), he learned that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla was at the Bodhi Tree (菩提樹), and the master of treatises instructed his disciple, saying: "Go to the place of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla at the Bodhi Tree and convey my words as follows: 'The Bodhisattva propagates the bequeathed teachings and guides the deluded; I have long looked up to your virtue with a humble mind. However, because my past vow has not yet been fulfilled, I have been unable to pay my respects. As for the Bodhi Tree, I vow not to see it in vain; when I see it, I shall attain realization and be called the Teacher of Gods and Men.'" The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla said to his messenger: "The human world is like an illusion, and life is like a bubble; my days are consumed with diligent sincerity, and I have no leisure for discussion." Messengers went back and forth, but they never met. After the master of treatises returned to his native land, he sat quietly and thought: "If it is not Maitreya who attains Buddhahood, who can resolve my doubts?" Before an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩), he recited the *Hṛdaya-dhāraṇī* (隨心陀羅尼), abstaining from grain and consuming only water for a period of three years. The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara then manifested a wondrous physical form and said to the master of treatises: "What is your aspiration?" He replied: "I wish to preserve this body to await the sight of Maitreya." The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) said: "Human life is precarious and fragile, and the world is a floating illusion. It is better to cultivate superior and virtuous vows to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven (覩史多天), where you may pay homage and meet him more quickly." The master of treatises replied: "My aspiration cannot be diverted, and my heart cannot be divided." The Bodhisattva said: "If that is so, you should go to the mountain cliff south of the capital of the country of Dhānakaṭaka (馱那羯磔迦國) to the abode of the deity Vajrapāṇi (執金剛神). If you recite the *Vajrapāṇi-dhāraṇī* (執金剛陀羅尼) with utmost sincerity, your wish shall be fulfilled." The master of treatises then went there and recited it. After three years, the deity asked him: "What is your wish, that you are so diligent and earnest?" The master of treatises replied: "I wish to preserve this body to await the sight of Maitreya (慈氏). The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara directed me to come and request this; is it not in your power to fulfill my wish?" The deity then bestowed a secret method upon him and said: "Inside this rock is the palace of the Asuras (阿素洛宮). If you perform the ritual according to the Dharma and make your request, the stone wall shall open. Once it opens, you may enter and wait there to see him." The master of treatises said: "If I dwell in seclusion and see nothing, how will I know when the Buddha has arisen?" Vajrapāṇi replied: "When Maitreya appears in the world, I shall inform you." The master of treatises accepted the command and recited with focused concentration. After another three years had passed, without a single stray thought, he enchanted mustard seeds and struck the rock with them; the stone wall parted and opened wide. At that time, hundreds of thousands of people watched, unable to turn away. The master of treatises (śāstra-master) stepped across the threshold and announced to the crowd: "I have long prayed, waiting to see Maitreya (慈氏). Through the protection of the holy spirits, my great vow is now fulfilled. You should all enter here to witness the arising of the Buddha together." Those who heard this were terrified and none dared to step across the threshold, claiming it was a den of venomous snakes and fearing they would lose their lives. After he exhorted them repeatedly, only six people followed him inside. The master of treatises looked back to bid farewell to the crowd and entered with composure. Once he had entered, the stone wall closed back up. The crowd all lamented and sighed, regretting their previous words.

en_revised: The country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) is over 7,000 li in circumference. The capital city is over 40 li in circumference. The land is fertile, the climate is warm and hot, crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The population is prosperous, and the households are wealthy. The people are short and dark-skinned, and their temperaments are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and value virtue, honoring goodness and diligently cultivating merit. This country was originally an island of gems; it contains many precious treasures and is inhabited by ghosts and spirits.  Later, there was a king in South India whose daughter was betrothed to a neighboring country. On an auspicious day, as she was being escorted there, they encountered a lion on the road. Her attendants abandoned the girl and fled to escape the danger, but the girl remained in her carriage, resigned to losing her life. At that time, the lion king carried the girl away, entering deep mountains and dwelling in secluded valleys. He hunted deer and gathered fruit to provide for her in due season. After many years had passed, she gave birth to a son and a daughter; their appearance was that of humans, but their nature was that of beasts.   As the son gradually grew up, he had the strength to wrestle with wild beasts. When he reached the age of twenty, his human intelligence began to manifest, and he said to his mother, "What am I? My father is a wild beast, and my mother is a human. Since we are not of the same species, how could they have mated?" His mother then recounted the past to her son. He said, "Humans and beasts follow different paths; we should flee at once." The mother said, "I tried to escape before, but I could not succeed on my own." The son subsequently followed his lion father, climbing mountains and crossing ridges to observe his movements so that they might escape the danger. Once he had waited for his father to leave, he carried his mother and sister on his back and descended toward human settlements. The mother said, "We must each be cautious and secretive; do not speak of the origin of these events, for if people should hear of them, they may look down upon us." Thereupon, they arrived at her father’s native country, but the country was not that of their kin, and their ancestral line had already been extinguished. They sought shelter with the townspeople, who asked them, "From what country are you?" They replied, "We are originally from this country, but we were scattered in foreign lands; mother and son have traveled together to return to our old home." The people all felt pity and compassion, and together they provided them with supplies.  When the lion king returned and saw nothing, he pined for his children. His fury erupted, and he left the mountain valleys to roam among the villages and towns, roaring and thundering, violently harming people and animals, and cruelly destroying living beings. Whenever the townspeople came out, he would seize and kill them. They beat drums and blew conch shells, shouldered crossbows and held spears, and followed in groups like an army; only then could they avoid harm.  The king, fearing that his benevolent influence was not reaching the people, released hunters, hoping to capture the beast. The king personally led the four divisions of the army, numbering in the tens of thousands, to surround the forests and thickets, spanning across the mountains and valleys. The lion roared, and both men and beasts fled in terror. Since he could not be captured, the king subsequently issued a recruitment call: whoever could seize the lion and rid the country of this menace would be rewarded with a great prize to honor their distinguished achievement.  Upon hearing the king’s order, the son said to his mother, "Our hunger and cold have become extreme; I should respond to the recruitment, for perhaps I may gain something with which to support you." The mother said, "You must not speak like this! Although he is a beast, he is still called your father; how could you, because of hardship, commit such an act of rebellion and harm?" The son replied, "Humans and beasts are of different species; where then is the place for ritual and righteousness? Since we are already obstructed and hindered, what hope is there for this heart?" He then hid a small knife in his sleeve and went out to answer the recruitment. At that time, thousands of people and ten thousand cavalry gathered like clouds and mist, but the lion sat in the forest, and no one dared to approach. The son went directly before him, and the father became tame and submissive. Thus, out of affection, he forgot his anger; the son then stabbed his blade into the father’s belly. The father still harbored loving kindness and remained without resentment or malice, even as his belly was ripped open, and he died enduring the pain. The king asked, "What kind of person is this, that he is so extraordinary?" He tempted him with benefits and threatened him with punishment, after which the son fully explained the beginning and the end, detailing the entire situation. The king said, "How rebellious! If he would even harm his own father, how much more so would he harm those who are not his kin? The beast species is difficult to tame, and their violent nature is easily stirred. To remove a menace to the people is a great merit, but to sever the life of one's father is a rebellious heart. I shall provide a heavy reward to compensate for his merit, but I shall banish him far away to punish his rebellion. In this way, the laws of the country will not be compromised, and the king’s word will not be inconsistent." Thereupon, he fitted out two large ships and stored them with plenty of provisions. The mother was left in the country and provided for with the reward for the merit, while the son and daughter were each placed on a ship and left to drift with the waves. The son’s ship drifted across the sea until it reached this island of treasures; seeing an abundance of precious gems, he settled there. Later, when merchants came to the island to collect treasures, he killed the merchant leader and kept his children. In this way they multiplied, and their descendants were numerous. They then established a ruler and ministers, assigned ranks of high and low, built a capital and cities, and occupied the territory. Because their ancestor had captured a lion (siṃha), they cited this original achievement to name the country. As for the ship carrying the daughter, it drifted to the west of Persia (Pārasī), where she was bewitched by spirits and gave birth to a group of daughters; this is the origin of the present-day Western Kingdom of Women. Therefore, the people of the country of the Lion (Siṃhala) are short and dark in appearance, with square chins and broad foreheads; their temperament is fierce and violent, and they are cruel and prone to poisoning. This is because they are the descendants of a wild beast, and thus the people are mostly brave and robust. This is one account.  What the Buddha’s teaching records is as follows: In the past, in the great iron city of this precious island, there dwelt five hundred rākṣasīs. Atop the city towers, two tall banners were erected to signify signs of good or ill fortune; the auspicious banner would move when there was a lucky event, and the inauspicious banner would move when there was a calamity. They would constantly lie in wait for merchants arriving at the precious island, whereupon they would transform into beautiful women, carrying fragrant flowers and playing music to welcome and console them, luring them into the iron city. After the festivities and banquets were over, they would place the merchants in an iron prison and gradually devour them.  At that time, in the continent of Jambudvīpa, there was a great merchant leader named Saṃgha; his son was named Saṃghala. His father being old, he took over the family business and set out with five hundred merchants to enter the sea to collect treasures. Blown about by wind and waves, they happened to reach the precious island. When the rākṣasīs saw the auspicious banner move, they brought fragrant flowers and played music, coming together to welcome the merchants and entice them into the iron city. The merchant leader then engaged in joyful entertainment with the rākṣasī queen, and the remaining merchants each paired off with one, and as the years passed, they all fathered children. The rākṣasīs, their affections for their old partners having grown distant, wished to imprison them in an iron jail to wait for other merchants. At that time, Saṃghala had a nightmare during the night and, knowing it was not an auspicious sign, secretly sought a path home. He happened upon the iron jail and heard the sound of piteous wailing, so he climbed a tall tree and asked, "Who is it that is bound and suffering such grief?" They replied, "Do you not know? The women in the city are all rākṣasīs. In the past, they enticed us into the city for entertainment. Once you had arrived, they imprisoned us and gradually consumed us as food; now more than half are gone, and before long, you too will suffer this same calamity." Saṃghala asked, "What plan can be devised to escape this danger?" They replied, "We have heard that there is a heavenly horse on the seashore; if one prays with utmost sincerity, it will surely ferry one across to safety." Having heard this, Saṃghala secretly informed the other merchants, and together they looked toward the seashore, focusing their minds on seeking salvation. At that time, the heavenly horse came and told the men, "If each of you grasps my mane and does not look back, I will ferry you across the sea to escape this peril and reach the continent of Jambudvīpa, returning to your home country." The merchants followed these instructions with single-minded devotion and gripped its mane; the heavenly horse then soared into the clouds and galloped across the seacoast. The rākṣasīs (羅剎女) suddenly realized their husbands had fled; they told one another, wondering where they had gone, and each carrying her young child, they flew through the air in search of them. Knowing the merchants were about to reach the seashore, they called out to one another and flew off to find them. Before long, they encountered the company of merchants; with mixed feelings of grief and joy, their tears flowed freely as they covered their faces, sobbing and saying: "I am grateful for our meeting and fortunate to have wed such a fine man; our home was full of joy and we have long shared deep affection, yet now you abandon us to go far away, leaving your wife and child desolate—how can anyone endure such a heart-wrenching fate? We pray you, look back and return with us to the city."  The hearts of the merchants remained unmoved. The rākṣasīs, finding their entreaties of no avail, resorted to their demonic charms and employed every manner of deception. The merchants, overcome by love and unable to bear the separation, felt their resolve waver, and they all fell back. The rākṣasīs congratulated one another and went away, holding the merchants by the hand.  Siṃhala (僧伽羅), however, possessed deep and firm wisdom; his mind was free from attachments, and he succeeded in crossing the great sea, escaping this peril. Meanwhile, the queen of the rākṣasīs returned alone to the Iron City. The other rākṣasīs said to her, "You lack wisdom and strategy, having been abandoned by your husband; since you are devoid of skill and ability, you should no longer dwell here."  The queen of the rākṣasīs then took the child she had borne, flew before Siṃhala, and, exerting her utmost charms, enticed and pleaded with him to return. Siṃhala recited a mantra and, brandishing his sharp sword, rebuked her, saying: "You are a rākṣasī, and I am a human; humans and ghosts follow different paths, and we are not a match. If you press me hard, I shall end your life." The rākṣasī, knowing that her seduction had failed, flew through the air and arrived at the home of Siṃhala (僧伽羅). She deceived his father, Siṃha (僧伽), saying: "I am the daughter of a certain king. Siṃhala took me as his wife and we bore a son. We were carrying precious goods to return to his native country, but while crossing the sea, we encountered a storm and our ship was wrecked. Only my son, myself, and Siṃhala managed to survive. The mountains and rivers were difficult to traverse, and we suffered from cold, hunger, and hardship. Because of one word that displeased him, I was abandoned and cast aside, insulted with improper language, and reviled as a rākṣasī. To return home is to face a vast distance, and to stay here is to be a lonely, stranded traveler. With nowhere to turn, I dare to present my situation."  Siṃha said, "It is truly as you say; you should enter the house at once." Not long after, Siṃhala arrived. His father said to him, "Why do you value wealth and treasure while slighting your wife and child?" Siṃhala replied, "This is a rākṣasī." He then explained the previous events in detail to his parents, and his relatives and kin all joined in driving her away.  The rākṣasī then complained to the king, and the king wished to punish Siṃhala. Siṃhala said, "She is a rākṣasī, and her nature is full of seductive bewitchment." The king believed this was untrue, and being charmed by her beauty, he said to Siṃhala, "If you must abandon this woman, I shall keep her in my harem." Siṃhala replied, "I fear it will bring disaster. Since she is a rākṣasī, her only food is blood and flesh." The king did not listen to the words of Siṃhala and proceeded to take her as his wife. Later, in the middle of the night, she flew back to the precious island (Ratnadvīpa) and summoned the other five hundred rākṣasī demonesses to come together to the royal palace. Using poisonous incantations, they ravaged the palace; they ate the flesh and drank the blood of all the people and animals, then took the remaining corpses and returned to the precious island. At daybreak, the ministers and officials gathered for court, but the palace gates were closed and would not open. They waited and listened for a long time, but heard no human voices. Thereupon, they pushed against the doors and opened the gates, following one another as they hurried inside. When they reached the palace courtyard, it was silent and empty of people; there were only skeletons. The officials and aides looked at one another in dismay, wailing and weeping, unable to fathom the source of the disaster. Siṃhala recounted the entire story from beginning to end, and the ministers and subjects believed him, realizing that the king had brought this disaster upon himself.  Thereupon, the state assistants, veteran ministers, various officials, and senior generals inquired after those of illustrious virtue and sought out those of sublime character; all admired the merit and wisdom of Siṃhala, and they consulted together, saying: "How can the one who rules the people be chosen haphazardly? He must first possess merit and wisdom, and secondly embody sagacity and discernment; for without merit and wisdom, one cannot enjoy the precious throne, and without sagacity and discernment, how can one manage the affairs of state? Siṃhala is the very man. He perceived the hidden danger in a dream, was moved by the response of the heavenly horse, was loyal in remonstrating with his lord, and was wise enough to protect himself. The mandate of history is here; let us compose a new song of praise." The masses were happy to support him and honored him by establishing him as king. Siṃhala, unable to decline the offer, agreed to hold to the middle path, and after bowing respectfully to the assembled officials, he ascended the throne. Thereupon, he reformed the previous abuses and set an example of virtue. He then issued an order, saying: "Our former merchant companions are in the land of the Rākṣasas; their life or death is uncertain, and good and evil are indistinguishable. Now, to rescue them from their plight, we should prepare our arms and armor; to save those in peril and show compassion to those in distress is a blessing to the state; to recover precious goods and store up treasures is a benefit to the state." Thereupon, he organized his troops and traveled across the sea. At that time, the banners of ill omen atop the iron city began to shake; the Rākṣasīs, seeing this, were struck with terror and immediately unleashed their seductive charms, coming out to meet the men to entice and deceive them. The king, having long known of their deceit, ordered his soldiers to recite mantras with their mouths and exert their martial might with their bodies. The Rākṣasīs stumbled, fell, and were defeated; some fled to hide on isolated islands, while others drowned in the surging currents. Thereupon, he destroyed the iron city, broke the iron prisons, rescued the merchants, and obtained many jewels. He recruited the common people to move and settle on the treasure island, established a capital, built towns, and thus a kingdom was formed. He then used the king’s name as the name of the country.  Siṃhala (僧伽羅) is a matter from a previous life of Śākya Tathāgata. In earlier times, the kingdom of Siṃhala only honored licentious sacrifices. In the hundredth year after the Buddha passed away, Mahendra (摩醯因陀羅), the younger brother of King Aśoka (無憂王), abandoned worldly desires to seek the fruits of sainthood; having attained the six supernatural powers and the eight liberations, he traveled through the air to this country to propagate the true Dharma and spread the bequeathed teachings. From that time onward, the customs have been pure and faithful. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas and over twenty thousand monks, who follow the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. More than two hundred years after the arrival of Buddhism, each [group] specialized in its own field, dividing into two schools: the first is the Mahāvihāra (摩訶毘訶羅) school, which rejects the Mahāyāna and studies the Lesser Vehicle; the second is the Abhayagiri (阿跋耶祇釐) school, which studies both vehicles and propagates the Tripiṭaka. The monks are pure in their moral conduct, their concentration and wisdom are clear and bright, their deportment is exemplary, and they are numerous and flourishing.  Beside the royal palace is the Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth (佛牙精舍), several hundred feet high, shimmering with pearls and adorned with rare gems. A signal post is erected atop the temple, upon which is placed a large padmarāga jewel; its brilliant light shines resplendently, and when viewed from afar, it glitters like a bright star by day or night. Three times a day, the king bathes the Buddha’s tooth with scented water and powdered incense, either washing it or burning the incense, striving for the utmost rarity and splendor in his offerings.  Beside the Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth is a small temple, which is also adorned and polished with various precious gems. Inside is a golden Buddha statue, cast by a former king of this country to be of equal stature to himself, with the uṣṇīṣa adorned with precious jewels. Later, there was a thief who waited for an opportunity to steal it, but the heavy doors and surrounding railings were guarded with strict vigilance. The thief then dug a tunnel to enter the temple through a hole; when he attempted to take the jewel, the statue gradually grew taller and higher. Having failed in his quest, the thief retreated and sighed, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata practiced the bodhisattva path, aroused a vast mind, and made great vows, offering up his own life and body, down to his cities and kingdoms, out of compassion for the four types of birth, bestowing everything upon all beings. Now, how could his bequeathed image be stingy with a jewel?" "Reflecting on this, I do not understand the past conduct." The image then bowed its head and bestowed the jewel. Having obtained it, the thief immediately took it to sell. Those who saw it all said to him, "This treasure is the jewel from the *uṣṇīṣa* (頂髻) of the golden Buddha image of the former king. Where did you obtain it to come here and sell it?" They then seized him and reported it to the king. The king asked where he had obtained it, and the thief said, "The Buddha gave it to me himself; I am not a thief." The king, thinking he was not being truthful, ordered an envoy to go and verify it, and the image was still bowing its head. Witnessing this sacred miracle, the king’s faith became pure and firm; he did not punish the man, but instead redeemed the jewel at a high price, adorned the image’s *uṣṇīṣa*, and replaced it on the crown. Because of this, the image has remained with its head bowed until the present day.  Beside the royal palace, a great kitchen was built, preparing food for eighteen thousand monks daily. When the time for the meal arrived, the assembly of monks would hold their alms bowls to receive the provisions, and having received their food, each would return to his own residence. Since the time the Buddha’s teaching spread to this land, this offering was established, and descendants inherited the succession, continuing the practice until the present. For the past ten or more years, the country has been in political turmoil without a stable ruler, and this practice has been abandoned. The country is situated on the edge of the sea and the land produces precious gems. When the king personally performs sacrifices, the spirits present rare treasures. The city’s inhabitants and scholars travel back and forth to seek and collect them, and according to their karmic rewards, what they obtain differs. Depending on the pearls and gems they acquire, there is a set tax.
