en_revised: From the country of Draviḍa (達羅毘荼國), traveling north into the forests and wilderness, passing isolated cities and small towns—where bands of brigands harm travelers—one travels over two thousand *li* to reach the country of Konkaṇapura (荼建那補羅國). The country of Konkaṇapura is over five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit. The land is fertile and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are impetuous and fierce. The people are dark-complexioned and their dispositions are wild and violent. They are fond of learning and value virtue and the arts. There are over one hundred monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are several hundred *deva* temples, where followers of various heterodox sects live together. Beside the royal palace is a great monastery with over three hundred monks, who are truly outstanding men. In the great vihāra (精舍) of this monastery, which is over one hundred feet high, is the precious crown of Prince Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成太子). It is nearly two feet high, adorned with precious jewels, and kept in a precious casket. Every fast day, it is brought out and placed on a high seat to be worshipped with incense and flowers, at which times it emits light. Beside the city is a great monastery containing a vihāra over fifty feet high, in which is a sandalwood statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩) over ten feet high. On some fast days, it shines with divine light; it is said to have been made by the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (二百億羅漢). Not far to the north of the city is a forest of *tāla* trees, thirty *li* in circuit; its leaves are long and broad, and their color is glossy and smooth. In all the various countries, these are used for writing. In the forest is a stūpa, which is the site of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the four past Buddhas. Beside it is a stūpa said to contain the relics of the body of the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (二百億羅漢). Not far to the east of the city is a stūpa; its base has already collapsed and sunk, and it remains three *zhang* high. I have heard from the records of predecessors that it contains relics of the Tathāgata, and on fast days it sometimes emits a divine light. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here and manifested his supernatural powers to save the multitudes of living beings. Not far to the southwest of the city is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is said that the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi manifested great supernatural powers here to transform and save living beings. Beside it is a saṃghārāma, of which only the foundation remains; it was built by that Arhat.

issues: great mountain (Pravaragiri) → name not in the text; vihara (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) → gloss invented (大精舍)
en_revised: On the eastern border of the country there is a great mountain, with overlapping ridges and connected barriers, and layered peaks with sheer cliffs. Here there is a monastery situated in a secluded valley, with lofty halls and deep chambers, built against the cliffs and resting upon the peaks; its multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces lean against the rock and face the gully. It was built by the Arhat Achara (阿折羅). The Arhat was a man from Western India. After his mother passed away, he observed into which realm she had been reborn and saw that she had taken a woman’s body in this country. The Arhat then came to this place, intending to guide and transform her, accepting her according to her capacity. He entered the village to beg for food and arrived at the house where his mother had been reborn. When the young woman brought food to offer, her milk began to flow; when her relatives saw this, they considered it an ill omen. The Arhat explained the original karmic causes, and the woman then attained the holy fruit. Feeling gratitude for the grace of his birth and mindful of the workings of karmic conditions, the Arhat built this monastery to repay her profound virtue.  The great vihāra (大精舍) of the monastery is over one hundred feet high, and within it is a stone Buddha statue seventy feet tall. Above it are seven stone canopies, suspended in the void without any supports, with a space of more than three feet between each canopy. I have heard from the records of predecessors that this is sustained by the power of the Arhat’s vows; others say it is the power of supernatural faculties; still others say it is the work of medicinal arts. Upon examining the actual records, the cause remains unclear. The four walls of the vihara are carved with stone reliefs depicting the various causal deeds of the Tathāgata when he was formerly practicing the Bodhisattva path. The auspicious signs of his attainment of the holy fruit and the spiritual responses of his entry into extinction are all carved in detail, with nothing, great or small, left out. Outside the monastery gate, to the south, north, left, and right, there is one stone elephant on each side. I have heard from the local people that these elephants occasionally roar loudly, causing the earth to tremble. In the past, the Bodhisattva Dignāga (陳那) frequently resided in this monastery.

issues: *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) → gloss invented, 精舍 = vihāra; Pañcavārṣika for 無遮大會 is an interpretive equation (lit. 'unrestricted great assembly', mokṣa-mahāpariṣad), kept with note
en_revised: From here, traveling northwest for more than two thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). The country of Mālava is more than six thousand *li* in circumference. The capital city is more than thirty *li* in circumference and is situated to the southeast of the Mahī River. The land is fertile and rich, agriculture is flourishing, and the vegetation is lush and dense, with abundant flowers and fruits. It is especially suitable for winter wheat, and the people mostly eat cakes and parched grain. The nature of the people is gentle and compliant; they are generally intelligent and quick-witted, their speech is elegant and clear, and their learning and arts are profound. Within the borders of the five Indies, two countries place great importance on learning: the country of Mālava in the southwest and the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) in the northeast; they value virtue, honor benevolence, and are brilliant and diligent in their studies. However, in this country, both heterodox and orthodox beliefs are practiced. There are several hundred *saṃghārāmas* with more than twenty thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are several hundred *deva* temples, and the number of heterodox followers is truly great, most of whom are the sect that smears themselves with ashes. The national records state: sixty years ago, there was a king named Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多). His ingenuity and wisdom were brilliant, his talent and learning were vast and sharp, he cherished and nurtured the four types of birth, and he revered and honored the Three Jewels. From his birth until his death, his countenance never showed a look of anger, and his hands never harmed a living being. When elephants and horses drank water, he would have it filtered first, fearing that he might injure the life-force of the water. His benevolence and compassion were such as this. During his reign of more than fifty years, wild beasts became familiar with humans, and the entire populace of the country refrained from killing. Beside his palace, he established a vihāra (精舍), exhausting all craftsmanship and preparing it with complete adornment, and within it, he had images of the seven Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, made. Every year, he regularly held a Great Pañcavārṣika Assembly (無遮大會), summoning monks from the four directions to provide them with the four monastic requisites, whether in the form of the three robes and religious implements, or rare treasures of the seven precious gems. This tradition has been passed down through successive generations, and this noble practice has never ceased.

issues: He made a four-legged seat for them → 為座四足: he made these images the four legs of his seat (the point of his arrogance) (Beal: made them the feet of his chair; Mizutani likewise); A bhikṣu, having heard → 苾芻聞已: the (same) bhikṣu Bhadraruci
en_revised: More than twenty *li* northwest of the great city, one arrives at the Brahmin village (Brāhmaṇagrāma). Nearby is a deep pit; during the autumn and summer, despite heavy and persistent rains that last for ten days, and although it receives many streams, the water never accumulates. Beside it, a small stūpa has been built. According to ancient records, this is the place where a highly arrogant Brahmin fell into hell while still alive.  Formerly, in this village, there was a Brahmin who was naturally wise and widely learned, his scholarship surpassing that of the eminent men of his time. He had thoroughly investigated the profound mysteries of both internal and external scriptures, and the abstruse texts of astronomy and mathematics were as clear to him as if he were looking at the palm of his own hand. His character was noble and refined, and his reputation spread far and wide. The king held him in great esteem and respect, and the people of the country honored him. He had thousands of disciples who admired his way and were drawn to his influence.  He would often say, "I have appeared in this world to expound the sacred and guide the ordinary; neither the sages of the past nor the philosophers of the future can compare to me. People are all swept up in following Maheśvara, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and the World-Honored Buddha; they propagate their doctrines, paint their images, and vie with one another to offer them worship. Now, since my virtue exceeds theirs and my fame dominates the age, if I do not do something different, how can I manifest my greatness?"  He then used red sandalwood to carve images of Maheśvara, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and the World-Honored Buddha. He made them the four legs of his seat, and wherever he went, he carried it with him. Such was his arrogance. At that time, in Western India, there was a bhikṣu named Bhadraruci (跋陀羅縷支) who had attained the pinnacle of skill in logic (hetuvidyā) and had deeply exhausted the study of heterodox doctrines. His moral conduct was pure and refined, and the fragrance of his precepts was intense. He had few desires and was content, seeking nothing from the world. Upon hearing of this, he sighed and said, "Alas! There is no one left in this age, allowing that foolish man to dare to practice such wicked deeds." Thereupon, he shouldered his khakkhara staff and traveled from afar, arriving in this country, where he fully explained his long-held intention to the king. When the king saw his tattered robes, he did not feel any respect in his heart, yet he esteemed his ambition and reluctantly accorded him the proper courtesies. He then set up a debate seat and informed the Brahmin. The Brahmin heard this and laughed, saying, "Who is that person who dares to harbor such an ambition?" He ordered his followers to come to the debate grounds, and several hundred thousand people gathered to listen. Bhadraruci wore his tattered, old robes and spread grass upon which to sit. The Brahmin sat perched upon the seat he had brought, denouncing the true Dharma and expounding his heterodox doctrines. The bhikṣu’s clear eloquence flowed like a stream, arguing back and forth. After a long time, the Brahmin admitted defeat. The king then said to him, "You have long abused a false reputation, deceiving your superiors and confusing the masses. The ancient canons record that those who lose a debate should be executed." He intended to use a red-hot iron seat to make him sit upon it. The Brahmin, in dire straits, surrendered and begged for his life. Bhadraruci took pity on him and petitioned the king, saying, "Great King, your benevolence and propriety are known far and wide, and your praises fill the roads; you should spread compassionate nurturance rather than practicing cruelty. Forgive his inadequacies and let him go as he pleases." The king ordered him to ride a donkey and travel around to proclaim his defeat to the cities. The Brahmin, ashamed of this humiliation, became enraged and vomited blood. The bhikṣu, having heard of this, went to comfort him, saying, "Your learning encompasses both internal and external doctrines, and your reputation is known far and wide; you should clearly understand the nature of honor and disgrace, and when to advance or retreat. As for fame, what reality does it possess?" The Brahmin, filled with resentment, bitterly reviled the bhikṣu, slandered the Mahāyāna, and spoke with contempt of the ancient sages. Before his words had even died away, the earth split asunder, and he fell alive into the pit; the traces of this event still remain.

issues: one hundred *yuta* (hundreds of millions) → 百億: a hundred koṭis (億 = koṭi, as elsewhere in DM); 'yuta' is unwarranted
en_revised: From here, traveling north more than one thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Valabhī (伐臘毘國). The country of Valabhī is more than six thousand *li* in circumference. The capital city is more than thirty *li* in circumference. The produce of the land, the suitability of the climate, and the customs and human nature of the people are the same as in the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). The inhabitants are prosperous and the households are wealthy; there are more than one hundred families who have accumulated wealth of a hundred *koṭi*s (百億). Rare goods from distant regions are mostly gathered in this country. There are more than one hundred *saṃghārāma*s, with more than six thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are several hundred *deva* temples, and the heterodox sects are very numerous. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled to this country; therefore, King Aśoka (無憂王) erected markers and built *stūpa*s at all the places where the Buddha stayed. The sites where the three past Buddhas sat, walked, and preached the Dharma are interspersed among them. The current king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is the nephew of the former King Śīlāditya of the country of Mālava and the son-in-law of the current King Śīlāditya of the country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國), and his name is Dhruvabhaṭa. His temperament is impetuous and his wisdom and strategy are shallow. However, he has pure faith in the Three Jewels. Every year he holds a great assembly for seven days, offering rare treasures and superior delicacies to the community of monks. The cost of the three robes and medicines, as well as rare and precious items of the seven jewels, are all offered in total, and then redeemed at double their value. He values virtue and esteems the worthy, follows the path and respects learning, and he shows special respect and reverence to high-ranking monks from distant regions. Not far from the city is a great monastery, which was established by the Arhat Ācāra (阿折羅); it is the place where the Bodhisattvas Guṇamati (德慧) and Sthiramati (堅慧) resided and composed treatises, which are both widely circulated.

issues: most of the inhabitants are followers who smear themselves with ashes → 天祠數十，多是塗灰之侶: [of the deva-temple people] most are ash-smearers (Pāśupatas); 'inhabitants' is DM's addition
en_revised: From here, traveling northward for more than nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Maheśvarapura (摩醯濕伐羅補羅國). The country of Maheśvarapura is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Ujjayanī (鄔闍衍那國). They revere and honor non-Buddhist paths and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma. There are several dozen Deva temples, most of them belonging to the ash-smearing ascetics. The king is of the Brahmin caste and does not have much faith or respect for the Buddha-dharma.

issues: keeping their traces far from the mountains and forests → 遠迹山林: withdraw far into the mountains and forests (sense reversed); Lesser Vehicle (小見; Skt. hīnayāna) views → 小見 = narrow views, not a term for Hīnayāna
en_revised: From here I returned to the country of Gurjara (瞿折羅國), then traveled north through wild wastes and dangerous deserts for over one thousand nine hundred li, crossed the great Sindhu River, and arrived at the country of Sindhu (信度國). The country of Sindhu is over seven thousand li in circuit. The capital city is named Vīṣanbhavapura (毘苫婆補羅), and it is over thirty li in circuit. The land is suitable for grain and crops, and is abundant in winter wheat. It produces gold, silver, and brass, and is suitable for cattle, sheep, camels, mules, and similar livestock. The camels are small and have only one hump. It produces much red salt, the color of which is like red stone, as well as white salt, black salt, and white rock salt; people in distant foreign lands use these as medicine. The people are fierce and straightforward by nature, frequently quarrel, and are prone to slander. They are not broadly learned, but they have deep faith in the Buddhadharma. There are several hundred monasteries with over ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sammitīya school of the Hīnayāna; for the most part, they are indolent, and their character and conduct are corrupt. However, there are those who are diligent, virtuous, and good, who live alone in quiet seclusion, withdrawing far into the mountains and forests, and who, without flagging day or night, often realize the holy fruits. There are over thirty Deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. The king is of the Śūdra caste; he is pure and simple by nature and respects the Buddhadharma. In the past, the Tathāgata frequently traveled through this country, and therefore King Aśoka built several dozen stūpas at the sacred sites. The great arhat Upagupta also frequently traveled through this country to preach the Dharma and guide the people; at every place where he stayed, he marked the remains, either by building a monastery or erecting a stūpa, which rise here and there and can be briefly described. Along the marshes and lowlands extending for over a thousand li beside the Indus River (信度河; Skt. sindhu), there are several hundred thousand households residing there. Their nature is fierce and violent, and they occupy themselves solely with killing. They herd cattle to sustain their lives, having no other means of livelihood. Whether male or female, noble or base, they shave their hair and beards and wear monastic robes, appearing like bhikṣus while engaging in secular affairs; they stubbornly cling to narrow views (小見) and slander the Great Vehicle (大乘; Skt. mahāyāna). I have heard from the records of the ancients: in the past, the people of this land were hardened and cruel, devoted only to violence. At that time, an Arhat took pity on their fallen state and, in order to transform them, came flying through the air, manifesting great supernatural powers and performing rare wonders to lead the multitude to believe and accept his gradual teachings. The people were respectful and pleased, wishing to follow his instructions. The Arhat, knowing that their hearts were compliant, administered the Three Refuges to them, calmed their ferocity, caused them to cease all killing of living beings, and had them shave their hair, dye their garments, and respectfully practice the teachings of the Dharma. As the ages passed and the world changed, their commitment to goodness wavered and their old habits persisted; though they wear religious robes, they have never possessed the precepts or virtue. Their descendants, generation after generation, have made this their custom.

issues: suitable for *śāli* (宿) and wheat → 宜宿麥 (CBETA punctuates 宿、麥): suitable for winter wheat; 宿 is not śāli
en_revised: From here, traveling northeast for more than seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Parvata (鉢伐多國). The country of Parvata is over five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circuit. The inhabitants are prosperous and numerous. It is subject to the country of Takka (磔迦國). There is much early-ripening rice, and it is suitable for winter wheat (宿麥). The climate is temperate, the customs are simple and honest, the people’s temperament is impetuous and hasty, and their speech contains vulgar expressions. They are deeply learned in the arts and sciences, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks, who study both the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings. There are four *stūpas* built by King Aśoka. There are twenty *deva* temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Beside the city is a large monastery with over a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahayana teachings; this is where the former śāstra master Jinaputra (慎那弗呾羅) composed the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā* (瑜伽師地釋論), and it is also the place where the śāstra masters Bhadraruci (賢愛) and Guṇaprabha (德光) originally entered the monastic order. This large monastery was burned by celestial fire and is now ruined and desolate.

issues: Sthavira school's Saṃmitīya sect (小乘正量部) → the text says 小乘 'Lesser Vehicle', not Sthavira; *śali* rice and wheat → 宿、麥 = winter wheat (宿麥)
en_revised: Traveling southwest from the country of Sindhu (信度國) for fifteen or sixteen hundred li, one reaches the country of Audumbatira (阿點婆翅羅國). The country of Audumbatira is over five thousand li in circuit. The great capital city is named Khāḍeśvara (朅䶩濕伐羅), and it is over thirty li in circuit. It is situated in a remote area on the western border, overlooking the Sindhu River and adjacent to the shore of the great ocean. The buildings are magnificent and contain many precious treasures. Recently, there has been no sovereign, and it is under the jurisdiction of the country of Sindhu. The ground is damp, the soil is saline, and foul weeds grow in abundance; the fields are little cultivated. Although all types of grain are available, winter wheat (宿麥) is particularly abundant. The climate is slightly cold, and the winds are fierce and strong. It is suitable for cattle, sheep, camels, mules, and similar livestock. The people are impetuous and do not like to study. Their language differs slightly from that of Mid-India. Their customs are simple and honest, and they revere the Three Jewels. There are more than eighty saṃghārāmas with over five thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle (小乘正量部). There are ten deva temples, mostly inhabited by ash-smearing heterodox ascetics. Inside the city is a temple of Maheśvara (大自在天). The temple is carved and decorated, the image of the deity is spiritually responsive, and ash-smearing heterodox ascetics reside within it. In the past, the Tathāgata traveled extensively in this country, preaching the Dharma to save people and guiding the commoners to benefit the world; therefore, King Aśoka (無憂王) built six stūpas at the sites of these sacred traces.

issues: much wheat and barley → 多宿、麥: much winter wheat (宿麥); CBETA reads 臂多縶羅 (縶 for 勢), DM's Piṭaśilā kept
en_revised: Traveling north from the country of Adhyavakila (阿點婆翅羅國) for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the country of Piṭaśilā (臂多縶羅國). The country of Piṭaśilā is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous; they have no great sovereign but are subject to the country of Sindhu (信度國). The land is sandy and saline, and the cold winds are biting and severe. There is much winter wheat, but few flowers or fruits. The customs of the people are fierce and violent. Their language differs from that of Mid-India. They do not care for the arts or learning, yet they are sincere in their faith. There are more than fifty monasteries with over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sammatiya school (正量部) of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than twenty Deva temples, all belonging to the ash-smearing heretics. In a great forest fifteen or sixteen li north of the city, there is a stūpa several hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It contains relics that occasionally emit light. This is the place where the Tathāgata, in a former life as a rishi, was harmed by a king. Not far to the east of this is an old monastery, which was established by the great arhat Mahākātyāyana (大迦多延那). Beside it are the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas, where stūpas have been built to mark the sites.

issues: the Tathāgata once listened to the bhikṣus wearing sandals → 聽諸苾芻著亟縛屣: the Tathāgata permitted the bhikṣus to wear boots/sandals (聽 = allow) (Beal: permitted the Bhikshus to wear…); millet and wheat → 宿、麥 = winter wheat; mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍) → gloss invented
en_revised: From here, traveling northeast for three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Avaṇḍa (阿軬荼國). The country of Avaṇḍa is two thousand four or five hundred li in circumference. The capital city is over twenty li in circumference. There is no great monarch; it is subject to the country of Sindhu (信度國). The soil is suitable for agriculture; winter wheat is especially abundant, while flowers and fruits are scarce, and trees and vegetation are sparse. The climate is windy and cold, and the people’s temperament is fierce and impetuous. Their speech is simple and plain, and they do not value academic pursuits, yet they are pure and faithful in their devotion to the Three Jewels. There are over twenty saṃghārāmas with more than two thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are five Deva temples, all belonging to the ash-smearing heretics.  Not far to the northeast of the city, in a large bamboo forest, are the remains of a saṃghārāma; this is where the Tathāgata once permitted the bhikṣus to wear boots (亟縛屣). Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; although the base has collapsed, it is still over one hundred feet high. In the adjacent vihāra (精舍), there is a standing Buddha image made of blue stone, which often emits a divine light on fast days.  Eight hundred paces further south, in the forest, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. The Tathāgata once stayed here; because the night was cold, he covered himself with his three robes, and the next morning, he permitted the bhikṣus to wear quilted garments. In this forest, there is a place where the Buddha walked for exercise. There are also several stūpas, arranged like the scales of a fish, which are the places where the four past Buddhas sat. Inside these stūpas are the hair and nails of the Tathāgata, which often emit light on fast days.

issues: great mountains (Pravaragiri) → name not in the text
en_revised: According to local accounts, to the west of this country one reaches the country of Kaikanan (稽畺那國); it is situated among the valleys of the great mountains, and it has separate local chieftains but no sovereign ruler. It abounds in sheep and horses, and among the horses are those of excellent quality, whose forms are remarkably large; they are a rare breed among the nations and are prized by neighboring regions.

issues: turmeric (*kuṅkuma*) → 欝金香 here is saffron (kuṅkuma = saffron; DM itself has 'saffron' in 12.01)
en_revised: Or the capital is the city of Ghasala (鶴薩羅城), the city circuit is over thirty *li*, and it is both steep, rugged, and well-fortified. The mountains and rivers are undulating, and the fields and ridges are high and dry. Grain crops are sown in their proper seasons, winter wheat grows in abundance, vegetation is lush, and flowers and fruits are flourishing. It is suitable for saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and produces the *hingu* herb; this herb grows in the Rāmēndu (羅摩印度) river valley. In the city of Ghasala, gushing springs flow in various directions, and the people of the country benefit from them to irrigate their fields.

issues: turmeric (kuṅkuma) → 欝金香 = saffron (kuṅkuma)
en_revised: Crops are sown in their proper seasons, winter wheat grows in abundance, vegetation is lush, and flowers and fruits are flourishing. The land is suitable for saffron (kuṅkuma) and produces the hingu herb; this herb grows in the Rāmēndu (羅摩印度川) valley.

issues: DM's bracketed identifications are not in the text and partly wrong: Great Snow Mountains (Mahāhimavat), Hot Sea (Rēgistan/Issyk-Kul), Thousand Springs (Bing-gyul), Huo (Kunduz), Wusha (Usha) → 大雪山, 熱海 (Issyk-kul), 千泉, 活國, 烏鎩國 only; Rēgistan is wrong
en_revised: From here, traveling east, one enters the Congling (Onion Mountains). The Congling are situated in the center of Jambudvīpa; they connect to the Great Snow Mountains (大雪山) in the south, reach the Hot Sea (熱海) and the Thousand Springs (千泉) in the north, extend to the country of Huo (活國) in the west, and to the country of Wusha (烏鎩國) in the east. They extend for several thousand li in every direction. There are hundreds of layers of cliffs and ridges, with deep, precipitous valleys where ice and snow accumulate permanently and cold winds blow with great intensity. Because they produce many onions, they are called the Congling; furthermore, because the mountain cliffs are of an onion-green color, they are named accordingly.

issues: the main hall (精舍; Skt. mūla-gandha-kuṭī) → gloss invented; 精舍 = vihāra
en_revised: The city of Khaṇḍata (昏馱多城) is the capital of the country. Within it is a monastery established by a former king of this country, who hollowed out the cliffs and filled the valleys to construct its halls and chambers. In earlier times, this country had not been reached by Buddhism and only worshipped heretical deities; it was only a few hundred years ago that the transformation of the Dharma began to spread.  Initially, the king’s beloved son fell ill. He exhausted all medical arts, but the illness only worsened without any sign of recovery. The king then went in person to a temple of the gods to offer rites and pray for salvation. At that time, the priest of the temple spoke on behalf of the deity: "He will certainly recover; there is truly no cause for concern." The king, hearing this, was joyful and comforted, and turned his carriage to return home. On the road, he encountered a śramaṇa whose demeanor was remarkable. Struck by his appearance and attire, the king asked where he had come from. This śramaṇa had already attained the holy fruit and, wishing to propagate the Buddha’s Dharma, had assumed this form. He replied to the king, "I am a disciple of the Tathāgata, what is known as a bhikṣu."  The king, being full of anxiety, immediately asked, "My son is afflicted with illness, and it is not yet certain whether he will live or die." The śramaṇa said, "The king’s ancestors may be raised, but your beloved son is difficult to save." The king said, "The heavenly deity said he would not die, yet this śramaṇa says he shall perish; how can the words of such a deceptive and vulgar man be trusted?"  Upon arriving at the palace, he found his beloved son had already died. He concealed the death and did not hold a funeral, instead asking the priest of the deity again, who still said, "He will not die; the illness will surely be cured." The king then flew into a rage, bound the priest, and rebuked him, saying, "You and your kind live together to foster evil, wantonly exercising power and claiming blessings." "My son is already dead, yet you still claim he will recover; such deceit and delusion are truly unbearable! It is fitting to execute the spirit-master and destroy the spirit-temple." Thereupon, he killed the spirit-master, removed the spirit-images, and cast them into the Vaxšu River (縛芻河). As he turned his carriage to return, he encountered a śramaṇa. Seeing him, he felt respect and joy, bowed his head, and apologized, saying, "In the past, I lacked a bright guide and lingered on evil paths. Although the corruption has lasted long, the reform begins here. I hope you will deign to look upon me and descend to my residence." The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and followed him to the inner palace. Once the son had been buried, the king said to the śramaṇa, "The human world is full of entanglement, and birth and death are in constant flux. When my son fell ill, I asked the spirit whether he would stay or depart, and the spirit spoke falsely, saying he would surely recover. Having previously received your instructions, which indeed proved not to be false, I see that your Dharma is worthy of devotion; I only pray that you will show compassion and guide this deluded follower." He then requested the śramaṇa to survey the site for a monastery (伽藍) and establish it according to the proper rules. From that time on, the Buddha's teaching flourished. Therefore, the vihāra (精舍) in the monastery was built for an arhat. In the great main hall of the monastery, there is a stone Buddha image, above which hangs a circular canopy of gilt bronze, adorned with various jewels. When people circumambulate, the canopy also rotates accordingly; when the people stop, the canopy stops. No one can fathom this spiritual manifestation. I heard from the elders that some say it is sustained by the power of a holy person's vow, while others say it is caused by secret mechanical arts. Observing the building, the stone walls are solid and steep. Examining all these opinions, no one knows the true account.

issues: great mountain (pravaragiri) → name not in the text; much pulse and wheat → 多宿、麥: much winter wheat (宿麥)
en_revised: Crossing the great mountains of this country, one arrives north at the country of Šikni (尸棄尼國). The country of Šikni is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is five or six li in circuit. The mountains and rivers are connected, and the fields are covered with sand and stone. There is much winter wheat, but few cereal crops; trees are sparse, and flowers and fruits are scarce. The climate is bitterly cold. The customs of the people are fierce and brave; they are hardened to slaughter and devoted to theft. They do not know ritual or righteousness, and they do not distinguish between good and evil. They are confused about future misfortune or blessings, yet they fear the calamities of the present life. Their appearance is coarse and unsightly, and they wear skins and coarse wool for clothing. Their writing is the same as that of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨羅國), but their spoken language is different.

issues: a large mountain (Skt. pravaragiri) → gloss not in the text
en_revised: From this valley, traveling southeast, one climbs mountains and traverses dangerous paths where there are no human habitations, only much ice and snow. After traveling more than five hundred li, one reaches the country of Kharbanda (朅盤陀國). The country of Kharbanda is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is built upon a large rocky ridge, with the Sītā River (徙多河) at its back, and it is over twenty li in circuit. The mountain ranges are connected, and the valleys and plains are narrow. Grain crops are scarce, but beans and wheat are abundant; trees are sparse, and there is little fruit or flowers. The plains and marshes are desolate, and the cities and towns are empty. The customs lack propriety and righteousness, and the people have little learning or skill. Their nature is fierce and violent, and they are also physically brave and valiant. Their appearance is ugly and wretched, and they wear garments of felt and coarse wool. Their writing and language are largely the same as those of the country of Khāsa (佉沙國). However, they are sincere in their faith and revere the Buddha-Dharma. There are more than ten monasteries and over five hundred monks, who study the Hīnayāna teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. The present king is simple and honest, respects the Three Jewels, is elegant and refined in his demeanor, and is devoted to learning. Since the founding of the country, many years have passed. The people claim to be the descendants of the *Cīnadeva-gotra* (至那提婆瞿呾羅). This country was originally a desolate valley in the Onion Range (葱嶺). Long ago, a king of Persia (波利剌斯) married a princess from the land of Han and was escorting her back when they reached this place. At that time, a military rebellion broke out, and the roads to the east and west were blocked. He therefore placed the princess upon an isolated peak, which was extremely steep and high, accessible only by ladders, and stationed guards around it to keep watch day and night. Three months passed, and when the bandits had finally quieted down and they wished to continue their journey, the princess was already pregnant. The envoy was terrified and said to his retinue, "The King commanded us to welcome his bride, but we encountered this rebellion; camping in the wild barrens, we cannot even plan for the next morning. Through the virtue of our King, the baleful atmosphere has now cleared, and we are about to return to the kingdom, yet the King’s bride is pregnant. Considering this, we are in distress, not knowing how to face death; we should identify the ringleader, perhaps to be executed later." They questioned one another with much clamor, but could not determine the truth. At that time, a maidservant said to the envoy, "Do not blame one another; it was a divine encounter. Every day at high noon, a man would arrive here on horseback, descending from the solar disc." The envoy said, "If that is the case, how can we clear ourselves of this guilt? If we return, we will surely be executed; if we remain, we will also be punished. Being in such a dilemma, what should we do?" They all agreed, "This matter is not trivial; who would willingly face such severe punishment? Let us await our fate outside the borders and delay for a while."  Thereupon, they built a palace and halls upon the stone peak, with a circumference of more than three hundred paces. They built a city wall around the palace, established the woman as sovereign, and instituted officials and laws. When the time came, she gave birth to a son, whose appearance was beautiful and refined. The mother administered the affairs of state, and the son assumed the royal title. He could fly through the void and control the wind and clouds; his majesty and virtue reached far and wide, and his fame and teachings spread to distant lands. Neighboring regions and foreign countries all paid him homage. When the king died at a ripe old age, he was buried in a stone chamber within a large mountain over a hundred li southeast of this city. His corpse was preserved like a mummy and remains intact to this day; resembling an emaciated person, he looks as if he were fast asleep, and his clothes are changed periodically while incense and flowers are constantly placed before him. His descendants have continued through the generations down to the present day. Because in the time of their ancestor, the mother was a person from the land of Han (China) and the father was of the seed of the Sun God, they call themselves the "Han-Sun-God Clan." However, their royal family resembles the people of the Middle Kingdom in appearance; they wear square caps as head ornaments and dress in foreign clothing. Later descendants declined and were pressured by powerful states. King Aśoka (無憂王) appeared in the world and built a stupa within their palace. The king later moved his residence to the northeast corner of the palace and used his former palace to build a monastery for the venerable Shastra Master Kumāralāta (童受論師), with lofty and spacious terraces and pavilions, and solemn and majestic Buddha statues. The Venerable One was a native of the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國). Brilliant from childhood, he renounced the secular world early, devoted his mind to the scriptures, and focused his spirit on the profound mysteries; he would daily recite thirty-two thousand words and write thirty-two thousand characters. Thus, his learning surpassed the scholars of his time, and his fame was high in the world. He established the True Dharma, refuted heterodox views, and his lofty discourses were clear and elevated; there was no difficulty he could not resolve, and he was universally esteemed throughout the Five Indias. The treatises he composed number several tens of volumes; they are all widely circulated and practiced, and he is the founding master of the Sautrāntika school. At that time, there was Aśvaghoṣa in the east, Āryadeva in the south, Nāgārjuna in the west, and Kumāralāta in the north; they were known as the "Four Suns Illuminating the World." Therefore, the king of this country, having heard of the Venerable One's great virtue, mobilized his troops to attack the country of Takṣaśilā and obtained him by coercion; he then built this monastery to manifest his reverence.

issues: the Great Mountain (Pravaragiri) → name not in the text
en_revised: Two hundred or more *li* west of the city, one arrives at a great mountain. The mountain’s atmosphere is dense and swirling; clouds rise where it touches the rocks, and the cliffs and precipices are jagged and steep, as if about to collapse yet not falling. On its summit is a stūpa of imposing and extraordinary construction. According to local tradition, several hundred years ago, a mountain cliff collapsed, and within it was a bhikṣu sitting with eyes closed. His body was of great stature, his appearance emaciated, and his beard and hair hung down, covering his shoulders and face. A hunter saw him and reported it to the king, who went in person to pay his respects. The city’s inhabitants and scholars arrived without being summoned, burning incense and scattering flowers, vying to offer worship. The king asked, "Who is this person? He is so magnificent!" A bhikṣu replied, "This person with long, hanging hair and beard, clad in a kaṣāya robe, is an arhat who has entered the samādhi of mental extinction (nirodha-samāpatti). Those who enter the samādhi of mental extinction set a prior time limit; some say they will arise upon hearing the sound of a ghaṇṭā, others say they will wait for the sunlight to shine. With such an alert, they arise from their meditation; if there is no alert, they remain silent and motionless, the power of their meditation sustaining their body so that it does not decay. The physical body, sustained by morsel food, would perish upon emerging from meditation. It is proper to pour in ghee to provide nourishment and moisture, and only then strike the ghaṇṭā to awaken his meditative mind." The king said, "Is that so?" He then struck the ghaṇṭā. The sound had barely vibrated when the arhat suddenly opened his eyes and looked up. After a long while, he said, "Who are you people? Your appearance is base and inferior, yet you wear the kaṣāya robes?" They replied, "We are bhikṣus." He asked, "Is that so? Where is my teacher, Kāśyapa Tathāgata (迦葉波如來), now?" They replied, "He entered mahānirvāṇa a long time ago." Upon hearing this, he closed his eyes, looking dejected as if lost in thought. Shortly after, he asked again, "Has Śākya Tathāgata (釋迦如來) appeared in the world?" They replied, "The holy one who guided the world has already passed into extinction." Hearing this, he bowed his head again, and after a long while, he rose, ascended into the void, manifested supernatural transformations, and transformed into fire to consume his body, his remains falling to the ground. The king collected his bones and erected a stūpa (窣堵波) over them.

issues: a great mountain (Pravaragiri) → name not in the text; presenting a singular sight in both spring and autumn → 春秋一觀: looking the same in spring and autumn (evergreen)
en_revised: On the southern border of the country is a great mountain, with craggy cliffs and ridges and overlapping peaks. The vegetation defies the cold, looking the same in spring and autumn. Deep ravines and rushing torrents flow in all directions, and cliff niches and stone chambers are scattered like chess pieces throughout the rocky forests. Many people from India who have attained the fruits of enlightenment employ their supernatural powers to travel far and alight here to dwell. Because many Arhats have entered nirvana here, there are numerous stupas. Even now, three Arhats remain in the mountain caves, having entered the samadhi of mental extinction; their forms appear like those of emaciated men, and their hair and beards grow continuously, so monks periodically go there to shave them. In this country, the number of Mahayana scriptures is particularly large; of all the places where the Buddha’s teachings have spread, none is more flourishing than this. There are over ten works consisting of one hundred thousand stanzas each, and from this size on down, their circulation is truly vast.
